newsitem.title: UK: Aon deal unlikely to spark broker bid war.
newsitem.headline: Aon deal unlikely to spark broker bid war.

text.p: Aon Corp's acquisition earlier on Tuesday of Bain Hogg is unlikely to trigger a wave of consolidation among international insurance brokers, industry sources and analysts said.

"This doesn't significantly change any competitive pressures among the big six brokers...This is what they were going to do, make acquisitions among the middle tier," one industry source told Reuters.

"It's not a big move, like a Willis or a Sedgwick, which would have some sort of a trigger effect possibly. I don't see this as suddenly bringing life into a dull sector with rating levels seriously depressed and horrible over-supply," one broker source said.
"I don't think it'll have much of a knock-on because there isn't a major broking house that hasn't looked at the options for expansion in the last couple of years really quite closely."
"There aren't that many fair fits at a reasonable price. Just because one's gone doesn't mean there will be a knock-on," he added.
International distribution group Inchcape Plc earlier agreed to sell Bain Hogg to Aon for 160 million stg cash. Inchcape had said it was planning to demerge Bain Hogg by the year end.

Shares in Willis Corroon Group Plc and Sedgwick Group Plc -- along with Aon among the big six international brokers -- fell on the news. The other leading brokers are Marsh & Maclennan Cos Inc, Alexander & Alexander and the unquoted Johnson & Higgins.
Analysts said the lower share prices reflected market opinion that Aon's acquisition of Bain Hogg reduced the likelihood of its bidding for Sedgwick or Willis.
Sedgwick in particular has been seen as a possible takeover target after it said in the summer that it was considering merger possibilities.
The international broking sector is ripe for consolidation, analysts said, but added that this would not be easy against a background of falling margins and declining demand for their services.
Merging two large brokers would lead to cost savings, but would also create overlap problems and lead to many people, often seen as the greatest resource of a broker, leaving to join a competitor.
"Aon is being shrewd. They're taking out bits and pieces. Basicaly they're buying people with relationships," one analyst said.
